metadata.title: Dockworkers Strike Against Arms Shipments at More Than 100 Ports Globally

sources.news_title: A global port strike could freeze $2 billion in freight
sources.text:
In a global labor action of record scale, dockworkers in 22 countries will strike on Friday to protest the use of their ports for arms exports. Organizers say that the strike, organized by an international coalition of dockworkers’ unions, could disrupt as much as 40 percent of marine cargo moving through the Mediterranean and bring more than $2 billion worth of freight to a standstill.
The strike, planned since May, has its epicenter in the Mediterranean: It was originally called for by unions in Italy, France, Greece, Spain’s Basque Country, Turkey, and Morocco.
Since then, port workers in Germany, Ireland, Portugal, Denmark, Sweden, and Australia have joined, supported by the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions. No national US-based unions have signed on to the strike, but groups of dockworkers in Oakland and San Francisco plan to participate.
The dockworkers’ demands, according to a statement released in May, include “an immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and recognition of an independent Palestinian state,” and an end to the US-Israeli war on Iran.
“Ports must not be used for the transport of arms, ammunition, military equipment or troops destined for war zones,” the unions wrote. At an October 15 press conference, representatives of participating unions estimated that even a single day’s shipping delay could result in $43 million in lost profit.
The people who load and unload cargo ships make up a class of workers with unusual power over foreign affairs and trade. Ships carry some 80 percent of all international trade by volume, and wars cannot continue without raw material—bullets, armaments, bombs, and fuel. Much of that cargo moves by sea, as it can be dangerous to ship by air, as analyst Francesco Vignarca of the Italian Peace and Disarmament Network told the Spanish publication El Diario this week. Europe has invested heavily in weapons over the past five years, and now imports a third of the world’s arms.
But, Vignarca said, “There is also a heightened awareness among workers—dockworkers, and others—which has led to more frequent protests, blockades, and a clear desire to put an end to this phenomenon.”
The history of dockworkers’ strikes is long, and studded with strikes like this one, which at times aim not only to increase workers’ wages or decrease their working hours, but to end wars.
Past dockworkers’ strikes in the United States have won bread-and-butter gains, like the 1913 longshoremen’s strike in Philadelphia, which shut down one of the busiest ports in the United States and won wage increases and better working conditions. Other strikes have disrupted the supply chains of war. In 1984, dockworkers in San Francisco refused to unload cargo originating from apartheid South Africa. And in 2008, 25,000 unionized longshoremen and warehouse workers shut down shipping along the West Coast of the United States as a protest against the war in Iraq.
Though activists in the United States have also attempted to target ports and stop weapons shipments since Israel began bombarding Gaza in October 2023, those efforts—which rarely involve the people who work in those shipping hubs—have seen limited success.
But internationally, port truckers, metalworkers, and dockworkers have found some strategies to stop arms shipments. Workers across Europe successfully coordinated actions to stop weapons shipments to Saudi Arabia in 2019, as that country was bombing Yemen; in 2024, dockworkers in Greece’s port of Piraeus stopped a shipment carrying arms to Israel.
“We will not let the port become an outpost of the US, NATO or the EU,” Markos Bekris, president of the Greek port’s container handling workers’ union, said at the time. “Our goal is to block the unloading in practice and prevent the transport of this deadly cargo. We will not stain our hands with blood.”

sources.news_title: ASRA NOMANI: 106 far-left groups in 'red-green' alliance target global ports
sources.text:
Communist revolutionaries, socialist activists and pro-Palestinian agitators from a network of 106 organizations are preparing to stage a carefully choreographed spectacle of global unrest Friday at ports from Oakland, Calif., to Mumbai, India, as they protest Israel and "capitalist barbarism."
A Fox News Digital investigation reveals that, far from a spontaneous eruption of outrage, the worldwide mobilization has been meticulously organized, with groups in the so-called "red-green" alliance of communist, socialist and pro-Palestinian movements spending the past week coordinating strikes, demonstrations and publicity around a common international playbook.
Organizers are targeting 113 ports across 22 countries and regions on five continents, seeking to transform the world's commercial shipping hubs into stages for a synchronized show of opposition to Israel, NATO, Western military policies and the global capitalist system.
CHAOS INC.: WHO'S WHO IN THE RED-GREEN ALLIANCE, INCLUDING NEW OCT. 30 PORT ACTION
The planned mobilizations – framed as "No Harbour for Genocide" with a sophisticated online tracker – stretches from Genoa and Livorno, Italy, to Piraeus, Greece, near Athens; Hamburg, Germany; Tangier, Morocco; Veracruz, Mexico; and Oakland and Marseille.
The geographic sweep is part of the strategy, synchronizing actions across continents, giving them a common message and turning scattered demonstrations into the appearance of a worldwide uprising.
In the "red-green" alliance, red symbolizes the far-left and green captures the color of Islam. The same network is set to bring a new round of protests, called "Acte III," to the streets of France on Saturday.
In the U.S., the international mobilization will spill into the San Francisco Bay Area, where ILWU Local 10 is activating its members to join the protest. An anonymous purchaser registered NoHarbourForGenocide.com in March 2025, according to online records.
The campaign's online infrastructure offers another window into the advance planning behind the protests, providing a common platform for actions that organizers intend to unfold simultaneously around the world.
Globally, the same network of communists and pro-Palestinian groups is fueling protests in India, Germany, Spain, Albania, the U.S., Australia and elsewhere, framing a more sanitized narrative of the protests as "youth" and "student" actions even though a Fox News Digital investigation has established that only about one in three groups in hotspots like France are youth-led.
The port mobilization represents the next stage of that international protest strategy, moving beyond city streets and campuses to the commercial infrastructure that connects the global economy.
In this case, communist and far-left dockworker unions and groups are joining forces with anti-Israel groups that have been using ports to literally set sail on campaigns like the "Global Sumud Flotilla," which sends ships to Israel in a show of protest theater. The so-called flotillas usually end with the Israel military boarding the boats and detaining protesters, which have included environmental activist Greta Thunberg. Typically, the detainees splash selfie photos and videos across social media from the sea and on land as a show of force.
The maritime confrontations have provided a visual and tactical precedent for international actions, combining disruptions at sea with demonstrations on land and publicity campaigns online.
GRETA THUNBERG JOINS PARIS PROTESTS, UNDERSCORING RADICAL THREE-WAY ALLIANCE
The planned protests reveal how agitators globally use every transportation corridor to disrupt civil societies, moving protests from streets, bridges and tunnels to ports, docks and waterways. This past week, activists associated with the Global Sumud Flotilla used three sailboats to confront the Sunaid X, a vessel that local unions identified as supplying the American military installation at Sigonella, Sicily. The report described the action as an attempted maritime blockade. Italian authorities seized the sailboats, and the activists were reported to prosecutors for allegedly disrupting a public service.
As the dockworkers prepare for Friday's actions, another part of the operation is unfolding far from the waterfront with an international publicity campaign that connects the demonstrations to a broader ideological struggle of communism and socialism against Western governments and capitalism.
In the march to the actions on Friday, pro-communist nonprofits in the U.S. funded by American-born Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham are amplifying the international campaign as communist and pro-Palestinian groups and labor unions create a cacophony of noise.
Last week, BreakThrough News, a pro-communist media platform funded by Singham, reported on the international dockworkers' strike, saying Italian port workers are "set to play a notable role." It placed the waterfront action within a larger narrative about student activism, "austerity," government policies and political unrest.
The publicity campaign also extends into a wider international ecosystem of pro-communist organizations, including one that has moved beyond publishing articles to raising financial support for the strikers.
Meanwhile, Progressive International, a pro-communist group that works closely with Singham-funded organizations, for example, supporting the Communist Party of Cuba, has published a series of reports and declarations promoting awareness of the dockworkers' mobilization. It published a trade union statement, called the "Istanbul Declaration," under the headline "Dockworkers will not become a link in the chain of their wars."
The Istanbul Declaration, issued earlier this year, proclaimed: "We do not load death."
Progressive International announced it has launched a strike fund to support dockworkers participating in the Oct. 30 action to "stop the imperialist war machine." It connected the port campaign to political causes beyond Gaza, including opposition to American and European policies involving Iran, Yemen, Cuba, Venezuela and "imperialism's entire coercive apparatus."
The international messaging has been reinforced by communist organizations that make no secret of their revolutionary objectives, using the dockworkers' campaign to advance a broader political struggle against capitalism.
On Monday, Italy's Rete dei Comunisti, or Network of Communists, issued another declaration tagged "COMMUNIST NETWORK," backing the strike and identifying the "task of communists" as fighting "barbarie capitalista," or "capitalist barbarism."
That day, Progressive International published an account of Italian dockworkers learning how to "jam the war marchine" in Livorno.
On Wednesday, 13 communist youth organizations from 12 European countries issued a joint statement explicitly supporting the international strike, saying, "We strengthen our struggle throughout Europe against our common enemy, capitalism," and calling for a "socialist-communist society."
Together, the statements show how communist organizations are connecting Friday's labor action to the wave of student protests already unfolding across Europe, giving the separate demonstrations a common ideological message.
On the eve of the protests, pro-communist, anti-Israel groups are drumming up international publicity for the waterfront campaign.
Thursday, the Communist Party of Greece, known as KKE, said it's dispatching its members to ports on Friday, declaring: "The communists support the strike." Its mission states that its objective is the "overthrow of capitalism and the construction of socialism-communism."
FIFTY ANTIFA GROUPS IN FRANCE JOIN VAST NETWORK TO ENSURE CHAOS IN WEEKEND PROTESTS
The Greek communists shared a statement from European Communist Action, in which the coalition of communist groups in Europe and the European Union linked the dockworkers' action to student protests in France, Spain, Italy, Belgium, Greece and Albania, connecting the pro-communist movements that have unfolded across the world in recent weeks.
Progressive International published a report Thursday on dockworkers in the Italian city of Gioia Tauro joining tomorrow's protests after weeks of collaborating with anti-Israel activists on actions that have been "stopping war cargo."
The campaign's international publicity also extends to Jacobin, a socialist publication that carried an article by a far-left historian, Peter Cole, headlined "Dockworkers Worldwide Are About to Strike for Palestine."
Singham, the Shanghai-based tech entrepreneuer, has been the subject of scrutiny over financial relationships involving nonprofit organizations and left-wing media operations that have coordinated and amplified anti-West protests in the U.S. and abroad over the past decade. In 2017, Singham sold a company that he founded, Thoughtworks, for an estimated $785 million and, according to a Fox News Digital investigation, pumped $285 million into a global network of pro-China, pro–communist organizations that have been key players in the past decade's anti-West protests.
The network associated with him includes BreakThrough News, the People's Forum and Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research. His wife, Jodie Evans, is a co-founder of CodePink.
DOJ LAUNCHES GRAND JURY PROBE INTO MARXIST MOGUL NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S FUNDING OF LEFTIST GROUPS
The Palestinian labor movement has provided the "green" in the international organizing network. This week, 17 Palestinian labor and professional organizations in the Boycott, Divest and Sanctions movement against Israel endorsed Friday's mobilization, urging dockworkers and transportation workers to join actions opposing military shipments to Israel.
The signatories include the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions, Palestinian Federation of Trade Unions, General Union of Palestinian Workers, General Union of Palestinian Women and Palestinian teachers' and postal workers' organizations.
Soon after, communist groups around the world shared the endorsement by the Palestinian groups, bringing the red-green alliance full circle.

sources.news_title: “Instruments of Death”: How Gioia Tauro Dockworkers Fight Arms Shipments at a Port Designed for Isolation
sources.text:
Macrì worked inside the port for about 20 years until the terminal's operator, Medcenter Container Terminal (MCT), fired him in February 2023. He calls it a political dismissal, and he is challenging it in court. "They don't let you in," he said. "There's a turnstile system; the badge doesn't open, and you stay outside."
Since his firing, he continued to organize the port's workers from the outside. He showed me around the surroundings of the terminal without either of us setting foot inside its fences: the quay, the container stacks, the rail gate, the empty and undeveloped industrial zone, the remote beach, and the winding neighborhoods that stretch north to San Ferdinando. Afterward, he drove south to Reggio Calabria to help organize Friday’s strike with schools and other civil organizations.
Beneath the cranes, 17 containers of steel are somewhere among the terminal’s countless stacks. The containers are from India, the unions say, and they were initially bound for Israel. "We managed to intercept and block containers holding ballistic steel, dual-use steel," Macrì said, "and 17 of those containers are still held here inside the terminal."
"They're ordinary steel bars," said Peppe Marra, a leader of the rank-and-file union USB, the next day at the union's office in Reggio Calabria. "But we know that, at their destination, they would have become bullets."
The steel has not been seized. Customs, which has classified it as dual-use, is holding it while Italy's arms-export authority, UAMA, decides whether it can travel onwards. "It's true they're not seized," Marra said, "but it's also true they can't be loaded." Domenico Lucano, a member of the European Parliament, has asked authorities to seize all 17.
On Friday, dockworkers' unions at 113 ports in 22 countries and regions plan to strike or stop work against war and the militarization of ports, according to Ports in Action, the coalition helping to organize actions on October 30. Gioia Tauro is one of nine Italian ports on the list; ORSA Porti and USB have called a 24-hour strike there, and USB called a general strike across every sector.
"Today we can officially say it's the whole world," Macrì said, "because the fifth continent, the one that was missing, has joined." Having held up the 17 containers is part of why Gioia Tauro is joining, he said: it was the "first result" that showed what the unions were able to do.
In Livorno, as I reported this week, dockworkers have worked out a method for stopping war cargo: find out what is really on a ship, picket it, and strike if it tries to load. The method depends on knowing which box, which ship, is headed for a war. "Livorno and Genoa organize differently," Marra said, "because here it's exclusively transshipment."
Transshipment means a container comes off a big ship, waits in a customs zone, and goes out on a smaller one without ever formally entering Italy. In 2025, Gioia Tauro’s terminal moved a record 4.5 million standard 20-foot containers' worth of cargo—more than 12,000 a day.
"It's the sheer volume of goods that lets so-called dual-use material blend in," Macrì said. On the quay, dockworkers "often don't know what's in the containers, unless the markings outside match, and you have to check they haven't been faked," Marra said. "A simple worker can't know the contents."
At Gioia Tauro, like the workers and organizers, the information also comes from outside. In the case of the steel shipments bound for Israel, the tip came through what Marra called "the whole international solidarity network against the genocide of the Palestinian people."
"We got the information through that network and activated our dockworkers inside the port, who immediately checked what could be checked," he said. "When we had confirmation, we filed complaints, started parliamentary questions, press releases, and pickets outside the port."
The first suspect containers arrived in March. Campaigners traced the steel to RL Steels & Energy in Aurangabad, India; BDS Italia said it was headed to a plant run by IMI Systems, an ammunition maker owned by Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer. By March 18, eight containers were under inspection, and Marra brought MP Anna Laura Orrico to the port. The transit of such material to a country at war, he told LaC News24, was "absolutely forbidden by our law." Macrì told the same outlet: "As the Piana, we are not complicit."
BDS folded Gioia Tauro into a Block the Boat campaign, and MPs and Lucano came to the gates asking to inspect the containers. They were turned away. On May 29, the movement went to sea. Five boats from the Thousand Madleens to Gaza coalition and Global Intifada sailed out in front of the port as the MSC Manasvi, a ship of the company that owns the terminal, came in to load eight of the held containers. The ship stayed offshore for hours, then turned back without them, organizers told Middle East Eye. "The Mediterranean is not Israel's," said Roberto Panza of the Cosenza activist group La Base, who was aboard one of the boats. "It is ours." That afternoon, solidarity groups and USB held a sit-in at the port gates, and several smaller base unions called a 24-hour strike. This year, an Al Jazeera investigation found MSC shipping goods from Israeli settlements.
By September, the count had reached 17, according to a union statement. On September 7, ANSA reported that a technical assessment ordered by prosecutors in Palmi, the Guardia di Finanza, and customs had found nothing criminally relevant in eight of the containers, and that the cargo would continue to Israel. The news site Fanpage reported the next day that the other eight hadn’t been checked, and that the shipment was booked for Haifa on September 14.
Marra rejects the premise. Israel, he said, "is a country at war that violates human rights. Either one of those two elements would be enough, and Israel has both. We absolutely cannot allow even the simple transit of war material in that direction." The law, he added, "requires establishing the end user and the end use of those bars. If the bars are for a safe or a car, that's civilian use, but it has to be certain and certified, not a simple claim."
The containers never left. On September 9, Lucano said all 17 were still being held: customs had classified the steel as dual-use and placed it under a "catch-all" review pending a decision from UAMA. In October, UAMA told him the files were still under "careful study and verification," and on October 24 he asked the courts to seize them. USB wants them confiscated. "After working so hard to block them," Marra said, "we don't want them to take another trip."
For the dockworkers who load the ships, it isn't only a legal question. "You find out that what you moved and loaded onto a ship would, a few days later, have become children, women, and men killed," Marra said. "We now have many foreign workers, sometimes from those very territories, who discover they themselves moved weapons to those territories." A moment later he added: "It's something that touches you. And if it doesn't touch you, you're not human."
On Gaza, Macrì was blunt. "Right now, a genocide is still under way. It has never ended," he said. What troubles him most is that "the world's powerful" know what is happening: "They don't want to stop this genocide."
Livorno and Genoa are old port cities. Gioia Tauro's container terminal opened in 1995, on the plain below the hill. "There was nothing here; it was all desert," Macrì said. The dockworkers commute from all over Calabria. "There's no port community like in the other historic ports," he said. The port is "too young in terms of port experience to have the consciousness you find in the historic ports—Livorno, Genoa, Trieste. That's why we struggle so much." Macrì thinks the scattering was deliberate: "wherever there are port communities, consciousness is born." Marra agrees: "These practices have been carried out scientifically, precisely to stop the workforce from organizing."
"When you finish work, you go home," Macrì said. "You don't stop at the dockworkers' pub to talk about the job." Marra described the same isolation from the union's side. Workers get to know whoever is on their own shift, he said; "otherwise it's hard to have real moments of discussion, workers' assemblies. Unfortunately, there's a tendency to eliminate these spaces more and more." Many drive long distances home after a shift, which, he said, "prevents the very socializing that is the basis for strengthening bonds between workers, and so for building union organization and having an impact inside the port." Gioia Tauro, he added, "has always been a preview. Whatever they want to impose to cut rights, they do it at Gioia Tauro first."
The terminal is privately run, but it has relied upon public money. Since 2019, MCT has belonged entirely to MSC, the world's largest container line, and it’s managed by its port arm TIL. MSC is headquartered in Geneva and owned by the Aponte family. MSC founder Gianluigi Aponte is worth at least $37 billion. When the terminal shed about 400 jobs in 2017, the government earmarked €45 million in public funds for a labor agency to absorb the laid-off dockworkers. To the unions, that makes the port a contest over whose interests public investment serves. Leave the ports to a few shipping families, Macrì said, and you risk leaving "the investment of entire governments, of entire states" in their hands. "We're returning to the dictatorship of the private."
Speaking up at work also carries a price. Supervisors listen to the work radios, Macrì said, and complaints about shifts or work pace bring disciplinary charges, framed as safety violations. He laid out what the company fears as a chain of consequences: "If you talk, you organize; if you organize, you react; if you react, the port stops; and if the port stops, it becomes a problem." In February 2019, dockworkers blocked the port for more than a week over the terminal's crisis and job security. "I'm still paying for that with my dismissal," Macrì said. "It came years later."
The two unions try to hold onto assemblies anyway. Both say decisions start on the shop floor. "The assemblies are sovereign," Macrì said. "If the assembly gives the mandate, it gets done." A worker who joins ORSA, he said, "wants to know, informs himself, then acts," unlike unions that cut deals with the company and present them afterward. At USB, Marra said, "the decision doesn't go from the top down but from the bottom up," and there is no secretary: "We have executives, not men alone in command, precisely to avoid personalizing the leader." The two unions work together at the port. "Only the acronym is different," Macrì said. "The thinking is the same."
Before Friday, that means explaining the steel shipments to colleagues. "We're trying to give information that's as detailed, truthful, and transparent as possible—to explain it to all our fellow dockworkers," Macrì said. "It's a response we have to give to the powerful of the world, who are trying to use dockworkers as instruments of death." For him, it is also a defense of the port itself. "It's a civilian commercial port, not a war port," he said. "We don't have military work contracts. We're dockworkers who move civilian goods, so we have nothing to do with wars, and we don't want to."
The port is one of the best jobs in Calabria, Macrì noted, and that makes people cautious. "The port gives you real economic stability," he said. "And that's also the fear." But, he added, "the fear can't be so great that we become instruments of death. There has to be a surge of pride from the dockworkers. There was one once, and I think there'll be one again, on a bigger scale."
On October 27, Transport Minister Matteo Salvini signed an order requiring that the strike be postponed in the transport sectors, maritime transport among them; some outlets read it as covering the ports. USB called the order illegitimate and said the strike would go ahead. Workers who defy it could face fines of €500 to €1,000 each. Marra reads the order narrowly: dockworkers "work ashore, on container handling. They don't fall under this order."
If there are fines, USB says it won't leave strikers to fend for themselves. "When we decide to give up a day's pay, we don't do it to take a walk or bring the kids to a café. We do it to protest," Marra said. "Those who were ordered back and still strike will have every possible support from our organization." Macrì called a strike "an investment" in his children's future.
The strike is being built beyond the port. "You have to talk with other sectors, other groups, and speak their language," Macrì said. "So we bring together representatives, 20 or 30 people, and they bring people in [for the 30th]." On Friday, dockworkers will march through Reggio Calabria, from Piazza De Nava to Piazza Italia, with students joining them.
On Friday, the 17 containers will still be in the stacks, waiting for Rome to decide what they are and what to do with them. Macrì has decided what the port should be. "A dockworker wants to bring bread home and look his children in the face," he said, "thinking that on the other side of the world everyone else is doing the same. As long as the port is not an instrument of death."

sources.news_title: Dockworkers Strike Against Arms Shipments at More Than 100 Ports Globally
sources.text:
Dockworkers Strike Against Arms Shipments at More Than 100 Ports Globally
Dockworkers in 22 countries will strike on Friday, protesting against war and the use of ports for arms exports in action organisers say could disrupt over 40% of Mediterranean cargo and snarl over $2 billion worth of freight.
The strike, originally called by dockworkers' unions in Italy, France, Greece, Spain's Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco, is now backed by more than 25 unions in 113 ports.
The protest is expected to target major shipping hubs across Europe and beyond, including Hamburg, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras, Piraeus and Genoa, as well as Morocco's Tangier Med and India's Nhava Sheva.
However, it was unclear how many dockworkers would take part or how severe any disruption would be. A spokesman for Italy's Genoa port said it expected only a limited impact, while Piraeus warned of disruption to ferry services for the Greek islands.
Among the labour groups joining the protest are ver.di in Germany, Ireland's largest trade union SIPTU, 3F in Denmark and CGT Ports et Docks in France.
Beyond Europe, the organisers said about a dozen ports in India could be disrupted, with the Water Transport Workers Federation of India (WTWFI) also supporting the action.
The Global Sumud Flotilla, a pro-Palestinian campaign group that repeatedly tried to break Israel's blockade of Gaza to deliver humanitarian aid, said it would execute "coordinated, strategic actions on the water" to support the strike.
Italian grassroots union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) called a 24-hour general strike in Italy for the same day, with protests scheduled in over 40 cities.
Ferries will remain docked at Greek ports on Friday as Greek dockworkers, engineers and seafarers' unions join the strike.
"We will send our own message of peace from Piraeus, and we will show our solidarity with the peoples suffering from war,” dockworkers at Greece's largest port, Piraeus, said in a statement, adding they would stop work from 0800 to 1100 GMT.
Other unions in the country will stop working for 24 hours.
'WE WILL NOT WORK FOR WAR'
In May 2026, dockworkers' unions from over 35 European countries published the so-called Istanbul Declaration demanding that port facilities not be used to transport weapons destined for war zones.
Italian harbours, with Genoa at the forefront, have played a leading role in protests against arms shipments, frequently blocking cargo shipments bound for Israel and for US military bases.
Over the 2021-2025 period, Europe became the world's biggest arms importer, data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute showed earlier this year.
"From planes to tanks, guns to bullets, explosives to ammunition, uniforms to boots, our ports have become replenishing and forwarding bases for war and genocide," unions said at a press conference announcing the strike.
Representatives of India's WTWFI said that about 15 Indian seafarers had died as a result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, with many more stranded at sea, highlighting the costs of armed conflicts on maritime workers.
($1 = 0.8925 euros)
(Reuters)

sources.news_title: Dockworkers at more than 100 ports to strike against arms shipments on Friday
Dockworkers From 100 Ports to Disrupt Military and Energy Supplies to Israel
sources.text:
Dockworkers From 100 Ports to Disrupt Military and Energy Supplies to Israel
The ‘international day of action’ is supported by the BDS movement.
by James Crump
28 October 2026
Dock and port workers from 17 countries will disrupt and block exports to Israel on Friday, with workers joining from countries including Italy, Mexico, Turkey, the US, Morocco and India.
Representatives from more than 100 ports will participate in the international day of action on 30 October, calling for an end to Israel’s genocide against Palestinians and “US-Israeli wars of aggression”.
The Palestinian BDS National Committee (BNC) announced on X that workers will take action by “peacefully disrupting and blocking the transfer of military, energy and other dual-use supplies to Israel, including by refusing to handle such supplies”.
Workers will also pressure governments to impose a full military embargo on Israel and end “trade, economic and academic relations serving its illegal occupation and apartheid”.
Explaining the day of action, the BNC said that Israel’s “criminal wars” are “exacerbating the cost of living and economic crises worldwide”.
“Military budgets are swelling in the colonial West, while families and workers struggle with the cost of health, housing, transportation, and education. Our struggles are interlinked,” it stated.
A further 17 Palestinian trade unions and federations have endorsed the action, stating: “Our struggle for justice in Palestine is inseparable from the global struggle against systemic racism, militarisation, exploitation, climate devastation and all forms of oppression.”
The day of action comes a year after dockworkers in Italy blocked the ports of Genoa and Livorno, with unions closing schools and stopping transportation as part of an Italy-wide general strike in response to Israel preventing the Global Sumud Flotilla from reaching Gaza in 2025.
The flotilla was the largest ever naval mission to attempt to deliver humanitarian supplies to Gaza, with around 20 vessels carrying delegates from at least 44 countries.
The flotilla was subject to drone attacks before being illegally intercepted by Israel in international waters. Those on board were detained and have accused Israeli forces of subjecting them to human rights abuses including assault, degrading treatment, and the withholding of medical care.
James Crump is a journalist.

sources.news_title: Dockworkers in Liverpool, around Europe will block Israeli arms in action against war
sources.text:
Dockworkers and other anti-Zionists and peace activists will hold a day of action this Friday, in Liverpool and other port cities around Europe, against the UK’s continuing support for genocidal Israel, the EU’s push for war on Russia, Iran and elsewhere and states’ war on essential social support and public services to make the warmongers rich.
Workers in more than 100 cities will work together to block the shipments of weapons and components, beginning on Friday 30 October.
‘Not their children, not ours’
In a statement promoting the event, the Liverpool organisers said:
Have no doubt: the UK is preparing for war. As a country preparations are underway. We are up to our necks in genocide already so don’t think it won’t happen.
Ordinary working people are paying the price as the money for our services NHS Education etc are cut to the bone. Join the international movement this Friday as dock workers across Europe and beyond call for an end to militarism, genocide, war and conscription.
Let’s stand together to give that message to our government. No to warfare yes to welfare. Workers won’t work for war – no to killing – not their children not our children.
The UK and EU are already participating in Ukraine’s attacks on Russia and trying to manufacture consent for all-out war, including conscription. 27,000 Ukrainians a month are being killed in the pointless war that could have been stopped a few weeks after it began in 2022. The warmongers must be resisted and defeated.
“This is what solidarity looks like!”

sources.news_title: International Port Strike on October 30 Against the Arms Trade and the War Economy - Left Voice
sources.text:
On October 30, port workers from various countries are calling for an international day of strikes and mobilization against the arms trade, the militarization of ports, and the war economy. The call to action aims to disrupt the logistics networks that supply armies and to denounce the role of commercial infrastructure in military conflicts, with a special focus on the genocide against the Palestinian people.
The mobilization is the result of international coordination among labor unions in the maritime and port sectors, which agreed to organize a joint day of action following the third International Meeting of Dockworkers’ and Port Workers’ Unions of the Mediterranean and Europe, held in Istanbul in May 2026.
The initiative brings together unions from France, Greece, the Basque Country, Turkey, Morocco, and Italy, representing workers from more than 40 European and Mediterranean ports. Various reports estimate that 57 ports are expected to participate in the international day of action.
The call to action represents a new attempt to shift opposition to war into the realm of direct action by the working class. Rather than merely denouncing military operations and government decisions, the unions propose to intervene in one of the material conditions that make them possible: the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment, and troops.
From the Ports to the Logistics Chain of War
The focus of the day of action is the refusal to turn ports into instruments of the military machine. The Istanbul Declaration demands that port facilities not be used to transport weapons destined for war zones nor be transformed into military bases serving NATO, the United States, or the European Union.
This demand comes amid rising military spending, expanding rearmament plans, and the growing involvement of transportation infrastructure in military logistics, while Israel presses ahead with its plans in Gaza. The argument is that maritime routes, warehouses, ports, and distribution networks are not spaces separate from war: they are part of the supply chains that sustain it.
Refusing to load and unload military equipment thus becomes a tool for exerting pressure. If war materiel depends on the labor of thousands of people to reach its destination, the collective action of those who perform that work prevents its movement.
The call to action on October 30 builds on a previous international mobilization, held on February 6, 2026, against the transport of weapons and the involvement of port infrastructure in military operations. The unions aim to establish stable coordination that will allow them to repeat and expand this type of action.
The day of action also has the support of the Palestinian labor movement, which has called on port, transportation, and related sector unions worldwide to join the mobilization, while respecting the leading role of labor organizations and the specific conditions in each country.
Italy: A Strike Aiming to Spread to All Sectors
One of the main focal points of the call to action will be in Italy, where the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) has called for a general strike encompassing both the public and private sectors. The mobilization also has the support of ORSA Porti, an organization that has joined the international coordination effort.
Extending the protest beyond the docks is meant to link the struggle against the arms trade with other sectors of the working class and increase pressure on the government and companies involved in the war economy. The goal is to ensure that opposition to rearmament and militarization is not limited to workers directly involved in maritime transport.
The Italian call to action is part of a history of mobilizations against arms shipments and the use of ports for military operations. The port of Genoa, in particular, has been the scene of protests and actions against arms shipments intended to fuel the Zionist genocide against Gaza.
International coordination aims to strengthen this ability to exert pressure, preventing companies from circumventing the protests by shifting operations to other ports or countries. Hence the importance of expanding the mobilization and coordinating union decisions on both sides of the Mediterranean.
The Struggle Against War Is Also a Struggle for Labor Rights
The October 30 action is not limited to opposition to the arms trade. The Istanbul Declaration links the struggle against war to the labor demands of port workers, who denounce job insecurity, the intensification of the pace of work, safety issues, and pressure on wages.
The unions are demanding real wage increases, stable employment, a reduction in the workweek, and decent pensions. They also reject the use of automation, artificial intelligence, and mechanization to destroy jobs, worsen working conditions, or undermine the rights workers have won.
These demands highlight a central contradiction: while governments allocate ever-increasing resources to rearmament and shipping companies seek to increase their profits, workers face pressure on their living and working conditions.
The militarization of ports also threatens to turn infrastructure essential to economic activity into spaces subordinated to the strategic needs of states and military alliances. For the organizing unions, defending ports as spaces for decent work also means rejecting their transformation into cogs in the war machine.
That is why the mobilization’s slogan, “Ports for Peace, Decent Jobs,” encapsulates two dimensions of the same struggle: halting the use of civilian infrastructure for war and defending the living conditions of the people who work in them.
The Global Sumud Flotilla Joins the Mobilization
The Global Sumud Flotilla has announced its participation in the international day of action on October 30, bringing the solidarity movement with Palestine into the initiative led by the port unions. Its participation aims to connect civil action at sea with workers’ ability to exert pressure on the logistics chains that sustain military conflicts.
The organization believes that the blockades, military operations, and destruction in Gaza cannot be understood in isolation from the commercial and maritime networks that supply the war machine. Its support for the day of action reinforces the convergence between internationalist mobilization and union action, although the call for October 30 stems from coordination among port workers’ organizations.
The Flotilla advocates for preventing public ports from continuing to be used for the transport of weapons and for protecting maritime workers exposed to the risks arising from military escalation.
Turning Solidarity into Material Force
The call to action on October 30 poses a challenge that goes beyond a one-off day of protest: building international coordination capable of influencing the trade and logistics flows that sustain the war.
Workers’ refusal to transport weapons can become a decisive tool if accompanied by union organization, solidarity across countries, and sustained mobilizations. The experience of Mediterranean ports shows that opposition to war can also be expressed from the workplace, challenging the economic interests that profit from it.
On October 30, the organizing unions are calling for a work stoppage and mobilization against the arms trade, rearmament, and the militarization of strategic infrastructure. This day of action seeks to unite the defense of labor rights with internationalist solidarity and opposition to war.
Because stopping the war machine also means taking action where it operates: in the ports, in the logistics chains, and in the workplaces that make its operation possible.

sources.news_title: Dockworkers in 22 Countries Prepare Coordinated Strike Against Arms Shipments Through Major Ports - https://eutoday.net
sources.text:
Trade unions representing workers at 113 ports across five continents are preparing coordinated industrial action on 30 October, protesting against the movement of military equipment through commercial shipping terminals. The mobilisation raises questions about international trade, defence logistics and the growing involvement of organised labour in geopolitical disputes.
Dockworkers’ unions in 22 countries and regions are preparing coordinated strikes and demonstrations on Friday, 30 October, in an international campaign opposing the use of civilian ports to transport weapons and other military supplies to conflict zones.
The mobilisation involves more than 25 trade unions representing workers at 113 ports, according to organisers, with planned actions extending across Europe, North Africa, Asia and the Americas.
Major shipping centres expected to participate include Hamburg, Genoa, Le Havre, Valencia, Algeciras and Piraeus, alongside Morocco’s Tangier Med and India’s Nhava Sheva.
The scale of actual disruption remains uncertain.
Some unions have announced 24-hour stoppages, while others intend to organise shorter walkouts, demonstrations or symbolic protests.
Organisers have suggested that the action could affect more than 40 per cent of Mediterranean cargo traffic and freight worth over $2 billion.
However, these figures represent estimates of potential disruption rather than confirmed losses or cargo volumes that will necessarily be immobilised.
A Campaign Extending Beyond Europe
The initiative originated among dockworkers’ organisations in Italy, France, Greece, Spain’s Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco.
It subsequently attracted support from unions in northern Europe and several countries outside the Mediterranean region.
Among the participating organisations are Germany’s ver.di, France’s CGT Ports et Docks, Ireland’s SIPTU and Denmark’s 3F.
Indian maritime unions have also declared their support, citing the effects of armed conflict on commercial shipping and the safety of seafarers.
The campaign follows an international declaration agreed in Istanbul in May 2026, when dockworkers’ representatives called for ports to remain outside military supply operations.
The organisers argue that commercial transport infrastructure is increasingly being used to facilitate the movement of weapons and equipment to active conflict zones.
Their demands extend beyond any single war, although opposition to arms deliveries connected with the conflict involving Israel and the Palestinians has featured prominently in earlier industrial action.
Italy at the Centre of the Mobilisation
Italy is expected to become one of the principal centres of Friday’s protests.
The Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) has called a nationwide general strike, with demonstrations planned in more than 40 cities.
Port workers are expected to participate in Genoa, Livorno, Trieste, Ravenna, Gioia Tauro and several other maritime centres.
Genoa has previously been associated with protests against the handling of military cargo, including shipments linked to Israel and American military facilities.
However, the port’s representatives have indicated that they expect only limited operational disruption from Friday’s action.
The distinction between planned participation and actual interruption of shipping is important.
Large ports operate through complex arrangements involving terminal operators, subcontractors, transport companies and different categories of employees.
Consequently, industrial action affecting one part of a port does not necessarily bring all commercial activity to a halt.
Greek Ferries Face Disruption
Greece is among the countries where the effects on passenger transport could be more immediate.
Dockworkers, engineers and seafarers’ unions have announced participation in the protests, with Greek ferry services expected to remain suspended for 24 hours.
At Piraeus, the country’s largest port, dockworkers have announced a three-hour stoppage.
Other Greek maritime unions intend to participate in longer strikes.
Disruption to ferry operations could affect travel between the Greek mainland and its islands, demonstrating how a campaign directed primarily against military cargo can also affect civilian transport.
The effects will depend on the precise participation of employees and the arrangements made by port and ferry operators.
Defence Logistics and Commercial Shipping
The planned mobilisation draws attention to the relationship between military supply chains and civilian maritime infrastructure.
Commercial ports are essential to international trade, but they may also handle military vehicles, ammunition, equipment and other cargo connected with defence operations.
NATO members and other states depend on commercial transport networks for certain aspects of military logistics.
Military equipment may be transported aboard commercial vessels or through terminals that also process ordinary goods.
The use of such facilities is not inherently unlawful, and arms shipments may be authorised under national and international export-control arrangements.
Nevertheless, dockworkers’ organisations argue that employees should have a greater role in determining whether ports are used to facilitate military operations.
This creates potential tensions between industrial rights, contractual obligations, national security priorities and government decisions concerning defence exports.
The implications are particularly significant in Europe, where governments are expanding defence production and seeking to strengthen military supply chains.
Any sustained disruption to port logistics could complicate the movement of equipment and components, although the consequences of Friday’s planned action cannot yet be established.
Europe’s Growing Defence Trade
The protest comes as European countries increase military spending and procurement in response to deteriorating security conditions.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Europe became the world’s largest arms-importing region over the 2021–2025 period.
The expansion of defence trade has increased the importance of transport infrastructure capable of handling military equipment.
It has also exposed disagreements over the political responsibilities of companies and workers involved in these supply chains.
For governments, the movement of defence equipment may form part of legitimate security commitments and international assistance programmes.
For participating unions, opposition to particular military shipments is presented as an extension of workers’ rights and their broader political objectives.
These competing positions are unlikely to be resolved through a single day of industrial action.
An Immediate Test for International Shipping
Friday’s mobilisation will provide an indication of how effectively unions can coordinate industrial action across different countries, legal systems and transport networks.
Its practical significance will depend on how many workers participate, which terminals suspend operations and whether shipping companies can maintain schedules through alternative arrangements.
The organisers have demonstrated their ability to coordinate protests across a geographically extensive network.
Whether that coordination translates into substantial disruption to international maritime trade remains to be seen.
For European governments and shipping operators, the immediate task will be to manage any interruption to commercial and passenger services.
The wider question is whether opposition to the use of civilian transport infrastructure for military logistics will become a recurring feature of industrial relations across Europe’s major ports.
